Q: Video streaming, How it works? A:

To answer the technical aspect of how video streaming handles data under the hood, it’s important to understand that chunks are typically stored in the client's RAM buffer or as temporary cached files in the application's internal directory to ensure smooth playback and seeking. After the stream finishes or the app is closed, most players automatically purge these temporary fragments to free up storage. For those interested in seeing how modified streaming clients manage these protocols or bypass specific player restrictions through request interception, projects like Vanced APK serve as an excellent real-world case study in Android-based stream handling and buffer manipulation.

Q: Core dumped, but the core file is not in the current directory A:

If you're missing core dumps for binaries on Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL) and when using abrt, make sure that file /etc/abrt/abrt-action-save-package-data.conf contains

ProcessUnpackaged = yes

This enables the creation of crash reports (including core dumps) for binaries which are not part of installed packages (e.g., locally built).

Q: Why x86 doesn't have conditional predicated execution like ARM's IT / ITT, and why no link-register for return addresses? A:

That's an interesting bit about segment registers. It's always interesting how things could've been but weren't.

Regarding segment registers - I think most of transistors there would not be spent on the registers themselves but on other things related to that (e.g. I guess there would be special instruction to change segment mappings in psw - as opposed to having pushf/modify/popf.. in fact there is no enough space for 3x3 bits in the flags register; and/or there would be more segment prefixes in opcode table and all that jazz). Whereas a specialized LR I think wouldn't require that much beyond flip-flops themselves. Not a GPR obviously - that would be a murder to do.

As for extra opcodes - they did ENTER/LEAVE in 80186 as a way to make prologue/epilogue more dense; with a bit of clarvoyance they could've done it in 8086, and used that to save/restore LR (either unconditionally, or maybe dedicate a bit in that second parameter noone uses and an extra opcode for LEAVE). That way most non-leaf functions (which at the time - at least in high level languages - had stack frame setup anyways) would have same code density and execution speed as they are now, and small leafs that don't use local variables would be somewhat faster.

Q: How can I generate a core dump in Linux on a segmentation fault? A:

Ubuntu 19.04 (Disco Dingo)

All other answers themselves didn't help me. But the following sum up did the job:

Create ~/.config/apport/settings with the following content:

[main]
unpackaged=true

(This tells Apport to also write core dumps for custom applications.)

Check: ulimit -c. If it outputs 0, fix it with

ulimit -c unlimited

Just in case, restart Apport:

sudo systemctl restart apport

Crash files are now written in /var/crash/. But you cannot use them with GDB. To use them with GDB, use:

apport-unpack <location_of_report> <target_directory>

Further information:

  • Some answers suggest changing core_pattern. Be aware, that that file might get overwritten by the Apport service on restarting.

  • Simply stopping Apport did not do the job

  • The ulimit -c value might get changed automatically while you're trying other answers of the web. Be sure to check it regularly during setting up your core dump creation.
